title: An Exosome Is Named By Its Origin

scenes.tts: A red blood cell that is nearly mature throws its transferrin receptors out of the cell. They leave still sitting in membrane, on vesicles about fifty nanometres across. A vesicle is a small sac wrapped in one membrane. For years this was read as rubbish disposal, but could it also be a message? First, where do these vesicles come from?
scenes.caption: A red blood cell that is nearly mature throws its transferrin receptors out of the cell. They leave still sitting in membrane, on vesicles about 50 nanometres across. A vesicle is a small sac wrapped in one membrane. For years this was read as rubbish disposal, but could it also be a message? First, where do these vesicles come from?
scenes.visual: A cell membrane across the lower frame, five blue receptors standing on it. They are thrown up and away, each inside a small teal vesicle; a vesicle is labelled and sized. Two dashed chips pose the puzzle (rubbish disposal, a message), then a dashed arrow runs from the vesicles back to a question-mark box inside the cell, which grows into the next scene's compartment.
scenes.narration: A red blood cell that is nearly mature throws its transferrin receptors out of the cell. They leave still sitting in membrane, on vesicles about 50 nanometres across. A vesicle is a small sac wrapped in one membrane. For years this was read as rubbish disposal, but could it also be a message? First, where do these vesicles come from?

scenes.tts: The answer starts inside the cell. The membrane of a compartment called an endosome buds inward, away from the cytosol, the cell's own fluid. It pinches off small vesicles into its own interior. These vesicles carry receptors. A compartment packed with them is a multivesicular body.
scenes.visual: The question-mark box becomes a large round compartment in the cell's yellow-tinted fluid. Its membrane pushes inward, away from that fluid, and pinches off vesicles filled with it, one after another; blue receptors appear on them and the compartment is named.
scenes.narration: The answer starts inside the cell. The membrane of a compartment called an endosome buds inward, away from the cytosol, the cell's own fluid. It pinches off small vesicles into its own interior. These vesicles carry receptors. A compartment packed with them is a multivesicular body.

scenes.tts: Picture this compartment as a sorting room with two doors, one to the incinerator and one to the street. If it fuses with a lysosome, its vesicles and their cargo are digested. But the same kind of compartment can move to the cell surface and fuse with the plasma membrane. Its vesicles are then outside the cell, intact, and those vesicles are exosomes. The word exosome therefore names an origin: a vesicle that formed inside a multivesicular body.
scenes.visual: The compartment shrinks to the left of the cell with a lysosome to its right and the cell surface above. Door one: it slides into the lysosome and its vesicles turn red and vanish. Door two: a fresh compartment rises to the surface, opens into the membrane and the vesicles float out, intact, and are named exosomes.
scenes.narration: Picture this compartment as a sorting room with two doors, one to the incinerator and one to the street. If it fuses with a lysosome, its vesicles and their cargo are digested. But the same kind of compartment can move to the cell surface and fuse with the plasma membrane. Its vesicles are then outside the cell, intact, and those vesicles are exosomes. The word exosome therefore names an origin: a vesicle that formed inside a multivesicular body.

scenes.tts: The direction of budding fixes the geometry. The bud forms away from the cytosol, so the inside of an exosome is a sample of cytosol. Its outer face is the face that was the outside of the cell. So a receptor keeps its orientation. The part that sat outside the cell still faces outward, as it did on the plasma membrane.
scenes.visual: A flat compartment membrane with three receptors standing in it, heads into the compartment, cytosol below. A bud grows up into the compartment, open to the cytosol and carrying the three receptors on its outer face; it pinches off as a cytosol-filled vesicle with its receptors pointing out. A plasma membrane on the right shows its receptors pointing out too; blue arrows mark both.
scenes.narration: The direction of budding fixes the geometry. The bud forms away from the cytosol, so the inside of an exosome is a sample of cytosol. Its outer face is the face that was the outside of the cell. So a receptor keeps its orientation. The part that sat outside the cell still faces outward, as it did on the plasma membrane.

scenes.tts: Cells also release vesicles that bud straight outward from the plasma membrane, called microvesicles. They are a different kind of vesicle by origin. But they have the same orientation, and they overlap in size. The usual markers of small vesicles, the tetraspanins, are found on both kinds. So once both kinds are in the culture medium, no agreed test reliably tells them apart.
scenes.visual: One cell surface. On the left a compartment has fused with it and an exosome floats above; on the right the membrane buds outward and a microvesicle floats off. Each carries an origin tag. Their receptors and orange tetraspanin markers match; then the tags go, the two vesicles swap places, and nobody can say which is which.

But they have the same orientation, and they overlap in size. The usual markers of small vesicles, the tetraspanins, are found on both kinds. scenes.tts: An exosome is defined by where it formed, and size, markers and orientation do not reliably show that. Showing that a vesicle carries a message is a separate job, and it needs controls. To call that vesicle an exosome, you must also show that it came from a multivesicular body. The field's own society urges authors to say extracellular vesicle unless they can show where a vesicle was made. So keep this rule: say exosome only when you can show where it formed.
scenes.visual: A compartment, an arrow and a vesicle labelled exosome. Three tests (size, markers, orientation) each get a question-mark badge and the note not reliable. A gold message arrow to a target cell is a separate job. A second row shows the same vesicle with no origin shown and the label extracellular vesicle; only the row with the origin arrow keeps the word exosome.
